newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Singapore, Taiwan libel suits expose divergent values.
newsitem.headline: Singapore, Taiwan libel suits expose divergent values.

text.p: A libel suit triumph by the leader of Singapore on Thursday contrasts with the outcome of a similar case in Taiwan, highlighting social differences between two predominantly Chinese economic powers, analysts said.

A Singapore court awarded Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and senior colleagues in his ruling party a record S$8.08 million (US$5.65 million) in libel damages after opposition politician Tang Liang Hong called them liars.

The verdict, which the court justified by saying Tang had made "malicious" attacks on Goh, came a month after a Taiwan court acquitted four journalists in a libel suit brought by the powerful business chief of Taiwan's ruling party.

Liu Tai-ying, who oversees the Nationalist Party's US$1.4 billion investment empire, sued the reporters of the Hong Kong magazine Yazhou Zhoukan on grounds they defamed him by reporting that he had offered to donate US$15 million to U.S. President Bill Clinton's re-election campaign.

Analysts said the contrasting verdicts showed that Taiwan values free speech more than its ethnic Chinese kin in Singapore -- but were quick to add that tolerance comes at the expense of social order in Taiwan's rambunctious democracy.
"In Taiwan you can pretty much say anything against the government and get away with it," said Chang Lin-chen, a law professor at National Taiwan University.
"But the flip side is you can also say -- and do -- a lot more really damaging things and get away with it in Taiwan."

Taiwan, which in the 1980s junked an autocracy in favour of pluralism, has prospered economically but also seen surging crime and other side-effects that make scholars and officials wonder if liberalisation has come too quickly.
The government has acknowledged that the island's social order deteriorated to "shocking" levels between 1990 and 1996, with the crime rate jumping 80 percent during that period.

Open anti-government displays -- complete with mass street rallies -- reached a recent peak over a spate of horrific and still-unsolved murders that culminated with the kidnap-slaying of a celebrity's teenage daughter.
On a more mundane level, Singapore's near tyrannical tidiness contrasts with Taiwan, where local media have bewailed one city's mountains of uncollected trash and the island's 1.3 million stray dogs.
Some analysts said it may be impossible for any country to maintain Singapore-style social stability while preserving the freedom of expression championed by full-blown democracies.

"If Singapore adopts democracy, all the social ills you see afflicting places like Taiwan and the United States also would come," said Tim Ting, a Gallup pollster and politics professor at National Taiwan University.
"Right now Taiwan and Singapore, being in different periods of historic development, simply value different things in their respective societies," Ting said.
